The first day at the hospital
It’s spring. Mihai has started working at a hospital in Madrid. In the evening, Ana calls him.
Hi, doctor! How was your first day? What have you done today?
Phew! I’ve worked ten hours. I’m dead tired.
Yes, I’ve met the whole team. They’re very nice.
This morning I had a meeting and then I saw fifteen patients.
Fifteen! And have you spoken Spanish all day?
Yes. The patients told me I speak very well.
Of course! You had an excellent teacher. Have you eaten yet?
No, I haven’t eaten anything yet. And on top of that… I’ve lost my house keys.
At my front door. My neighbour has called the locksmith.
What a day! Hey, have you ever tried cocido madrileño?
Then tonight you’re coming to dinner at my place. I’ve made cocido!
In Spain the d in -ado is very weak, almost disappearing: hablado ≈ “ablao”. Say it softly, but don’t drop it completely: that’s the clearest version.
The h is silent: he = “e”, ha = “a”, han = “an”. “He comido” sounds like “ecomido”.
Review the diphthongs: vuelto, puerta, siento — one quick syllable.
1. The pretérito perfecto: just like “I have eaten”
Great news: the first Spanish past tense is built exactly like the English present perfect. English: “have” + “eaten”. Spanish: HE + COMIDO.
English does exactly the same: an auxiliary + a participle that doesn’t change. “He comido” = “I have eaten”, word for word!
The auxiliary is HABER (he, has, ha), not TENER — even though English uses “have” for both. “Tengo comido” is wrong.
The rule is simple: -AR → -ADO, and -ER and -IR → -IDO.
A few irregular, very common participles must be learned by heart:
After HABER the participle does NOT change for gender or number: “Ana ha comido”, “ellas han comido”.
In Spain, the pretérito perfecto is used for things that happened in a period of time that has NOT finished yet:
Esta semana he ido al cine.
Este año he viajado a Italia.
Ya he comido. / Todavía no he comido.

Careful: Spanish uses it with “hoy” and “esta mañana” even where English would use the simple past (“This morning I had a meeting”). For “yesterday”, “last year”, “in 2010” there is another past tense (pretérito indefinido), which you learn in the next chapter.
In Latin America it is used less. Mexicans often say “Hoy comí” instead of “Hoy he comido”. Both are correct!
To ask about life experiences, combine the perfecto with “alguna vez” (ever) and “nunca” (never), just like English “Have you ever…?”.
Have you ever been to Mexico?
No, I’ve never been to Mexico.
Nothing goes between HABER and the participle! Unlike English “I have already eaten”, “He ya comido” is wrong. Correct: “Ya he comido” or “He comido ya”.
Pronouns (me, te, se, lo…) go before the auxiliary:
When he came to Spain, Mihai wrote a list of things he wants to do. Now he checks it.
When I arrived in Spain, I wrote a list of things to do. Let’s see.
Learn Spanish: done! I’ve studied a lot and I already speak quite well.
Visit the Prado Museum: I’ve already visited it three times.
Try paella: I tried it in Valencia. Amazing!
See a Real Madrid match: I haven’t seen one yet. The tickets are very expensive.
Learn to dance flamenco: Ana has given me three lessons, but I dance terribly.
Go to Barcelona: I haven’t been yet. I’m going in the summer.
Find a job: yes! This month I started at the hospital.
Make friends: I’ve met wonderful people: Ana, Kenji, Lena, Tom…
Read a book in Spanish: I’ve started “Don Quixote”, but it’s very long.
So far I’ve done six things out of ten. Not bad!
And I’ve learned something important: in Spain nobody ever has dinner before nine o’clock.
¿Por qué no ha visto un partido del Real Madrid?
¿Cuántas cosas de la lista ha hecho?
Kenji has lived in Madrid for three years. In that time he has done many things for the first time.
He has tried Iberian ham and he loved it. He has also tried snails, but he didn’t like them at all.
He has learned to have lunch at three in the afternoon and dinner at ten at night, like the Spaniards.
He has visited eleven Spanish cities. His favourite is San Sebastián, because there he ate the best pinchos of his life.
He has danced flamenco in Seville and run a half marathon in Valencia.
But most importantly: he has opened his own restaurant. At first he had lots of problems.
He didn’t understand the town hall paperwork, he lost money and he worked fourteen hours a day.
Even so, this year the restaurant has won a prize: “The best ramen in Madrid”.
There are still things Kenji hasn’t done. He has never seen a Real Madrid match at the stadium.
He has never been to the Canary Islands and he still hasn’t learned to make a good potato omelette.
Today Ana asked him: “Kenji, have you ever thought about going back to Japan?”.
Kenji smiled. “Yes, many times. But each time I’ve decided to stay. Madrid is my home now.”
This week Kenji has written a new list on the kitchen wall. It’s called “Things I haven’t done yet”.
The first item says: “Learn to make Grandma Rosario’s tortilla”. She has already promised him a lesson on Sunday.
¿Qué no le ha gustado a Kenji?
